en.title: Forestry and Wildlife: the whole course
en.short: What forestry and wildlife is, how the degree is organised, the main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Forestry and Wildlife is the study and management of forests, trees, wild animals and the habitats they share. It asks how to produce timber, fuelwood, food, medicine, honey and other benefits while keeping soil, water, biodiversity and carbon safe. Forestry usually focuses on tree-dominated ecosystems: natural forest, plantations, woodlots and agroforestry. Wildlife management focuses on wild animals, their populations and habitats, including protected areas, wetlands and rangelands. The two are taught together because managing one affects the other. The subject draws on ecology and botany, but also on measurement, economics, law, engineering and community work. It is not only conservation, and not only timber production; most real decisions involve trade-offs between several goals.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Length and award differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, forestry and wildlife is commonly studied within agriculture, renewable natural resources or environmental sciences. Universities award a BSc, polytechnics award ND and HND, and colleges of education award NCE; a BSc is often four years, but some programmes are longer. In the UK, a BSc is commonly three years (four in Scotland), sometimes with a placement year. In Ghana and Kenya, four years is common for a BSc. Always check your own handbook for duration and award. A typical programme starts with biology, chemistry, mathematics and introductory forestry, then adds ecology, measurement, silviculture, protection, wildlife, economics and policy. The final year usually includes a supervised project. A master’s degree goes deeper into research methods and specialised topics, and ends with a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually begins with foundations. You study the scope and history of forestry and wildlife, forest botany and dendrology (tree identification), forest ecology, soils and site quality, forest meteorology and microclimate, biometrics and mensuration mathematics, surveying, mapping and remote sensing, and tree physiology and vegetative propagation. These give the vocabulary and field skills for later work.

The core then covers nursery practice and silvicultural systems, plantation forestry, forest protection against pests, diseases and fire, tree improvement and seed technology, growth and yield modelling, inventory and sampling design, forest economics and valuation, and forest policy, legislation and administration. Wildlife follows alongside: wildlife ecology and population dynamics, wildlife management and habitat manipulation, protected areas and conservation planning, and wildlife census, monitoring and law enforcement. Forest-linked production is included through fisheries and aquaculture, apiculture (beekeeping), non-timber forest products and agroforestry, forest hydrology and watershed management, forest roads, engineering and harvesting, wood science and products, forest entomology, forest pathology, and professional ethics, extension and community forestry. Research methods prepare you for the final project.

At master’s level, common topics are forest biotechnology and molecular tools, forest landscape restoration, climate change, carbon accounting and REDD+ (reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation), and conservation genetics and advanced wildlife science.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text: Study with your hands and eyes as well as your notes. Learn tree and animal identification by repeated field practice, using local names alongside scientific names. Keep a field notebook with date, place, habitat, weather and what you saw. For measurement topics, work through calculations with real or realistic data: basal area, tree volume, growth increment, population estimates and sampling error. Check units at every step. Draw maps and cross-sections by hand before using software. Read policy and law from your own country, and compare it with one other country. Work in small groups for field exercises, but write your own records. Practise safe field conduct and obtain permission before entering protected areas. Use past questions and short weekly reviews; forestry rewards steady reading and regular field practice more than last-minute cramming.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Students often think forestry means only planting trees, or that wildlife management means only protecting animals. Both ignore the working landscape: plantations, farms, community forests and wetlands. Another mistake is to identify species from photographs alone; many trees and animals need field characters and expert confirmation. In measurement, students mix hectares with square metres, diameter in centimetres with radius in metres, and fresh weight with dry weight. In ecology, they treat a correlation as proof of cause. In policy work, they apply one country’s law to another, or ignore customary tenure and community rights. In field work, they record data without sampling design, so the sample is biased. Finally, they quote old statistics without a date or source. Check every figure and every rule against a current official source.

keyPoints: Forestry and wildlife is applied ecology plus management, measurement, economics and law.
Degrees and awards differ by country and institution; check your own handbook.
Learn species identification and field measurement by regular practice, not by memorising photographs.
Units, sampling design and data sources decide whether a forest or wildlife estimate is trustworthy.
Local law, tenure and community rights shape what management is possible.
Production and conservation are both goals; good management makes the trade-offs explicit.

en.title: Forestry and Wildlife: Scope, Terms and History
en.short: Definitions, scope, links to agriculture and environment, and the growth of forestry and wildlife in Africa.

sections.heading: Definitions and scope
sections.text:
Forestry is the science, art and practice of managing forests and trees for timber, fuel, water, biodiversity, recreation and livelihoods. Wildlife management is the management of wild animals and their habitats to keep populations healthy and meet conservation and human needs. It includes protection, habitat manipulation, sustainable use and law enforcement.

Silviculture is the care of forest stands. Conservation protects natural resources for present and future use. A protected area is land or water set aside for nature. Ecosystem services are benefits from nature, such as clean water.

sections.heading: Place in agriculture and environment
sections.text:
Forestry and wildlife sit inside agriculture in the broad sense: the management of land, plants and animals for human use. Many universities place them in agriculture or renewable natural resources faculties.

They also belong to environmental science, because they study ecosystems, biodiversity, climate and human impact. Forestry supplies wood and non-timber products; wildlife management supplies conservation, tourism and food. Both must balance production with protection.

sections.heading: Growth in Africa and Nigeria
sections.text:
Before colonial rule, African communities managed forests and wildlife through customary rules, sacred groves and hunting taboos. In the colonial period, British and other administrations set up forest departments and forest ordinances in West and East Africa. They reserved forests for timber and revenue and created game departments and hunting licences. Nigeria’s forest reserves and forestry department grew in this era.

After independence, governments expanded forest services, game reserves and national parks. Nigeria later created national parks such as Cross River and Gashaka-Gumti and a national parks service to manage them. IUCN was founded in 1948 and WWF in 1961. They support protected areas and species assessments in Africa. Community forestry and participatory management grew in the late twentieth century.

sections.heading: A shared land case
sections.text:
In a Nigerian forest reserve, a forestry officer plans a teak thinning while a wildlife officer surveys monkeys and checks hunting permits. Both use the same map and report to the state ministry.

Forestry asks about timber yield; wildlife asks about population survival.

keyPoints: Forestry manages forests and trees for products, services and conservation.
Wildlife management manages wild animals and habitats for healthy populations and human needs.
Forestry and wildlife are land uses within agriculture and part of environmental science.
Colonial forest departments reserved forests for timber; after independence governments expanded forest services and national parks.
IUCN (1948) and WWF (1961) are international conservation bodies that support protected areas and species work in Africa.
Silviculture, conservation, protected areas and ecosystem services are key related terms.

en.title: Forest Botany and Dendrology: Tree Form, Growth and Identification
en.short: Tree and shrub form, cambium growth, wood and bark, and identifying tropical African trees by leaves, bark and fruit.

sections.heading: Tree and shrub form
sections.text: A tree is a woody plant with one main stem, the trunk, that usually branches above ground into a crown. A shrub is woody but branches from or near the base and is shorter. Morphology is the study of outward form. Both trees and shrubs have roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruit and seeds. Leaves may be simple (one blade) or compound (several leaflets on one stalk), and arranged alternately, opposite or in whorls. These features are the first clues in identification.

sections.heading: How wood and bark grow
sections.text: Trees grow taller from apical meristems (growing tips) and thicker from lateral meristems. The vascular cambium, a thin layer between wood and bark, divides to make secondary xylem (wood) inward and phloem (food-conducting tissue) outward. Cork cambium makes periderm, the outer bark. In broadleaved trees (hardwoods), xylem contains vessels, fibres and rays. Sapwood conducts water; heartwood is darker and no longer conducts. Growth rings are not always annual in the tropics. Palms lack a vascular cambium and grow differently.

sections.heading: Reading leaves, bark and fruit
sections.text: Identify by several features, not one. Record leaf arrangement, whether compound, leaflet shape and margin, vein pattern, smell, latex and stipules (leaf-base appendages). For bark, note colour, texture, lenticels (breathing pores), and a slash (cut) showing colour and exudate (sap or latex). Fruit type and family features confirm. Example: Khaya species (Meliaceae, African mahogany) have alternate pinnate (feather-like) leaves, scaly bark and woody capsules (dry splitting fruits). Ficus species (Moraceae) have milky latex and figs, fruits eaten by birds, bats and monkeys. Parkia biglobosa (Fabaceae) has bipinnate (twice-divided) leaves and pods.

sections.heading: Names and classification
sections.text: Classification groups plants by shared features and ancestry. A binomial (two-part) name has genus (capitalised) and species (lowercase), italicised in print. Family names end in -aceae. Terms include indigenous (native), exotic (introduced), naturalised (established after introduction), variety (wild variant) and cultivar (cultivated variety). Common names vary, so use accepted botanical names and check current sources such as the African Plants Database or Plants of the World Online (POWO).

keyPoints: Trees have one main trunk; shrubs branch from near the base.
Vascular cambium makes xylem inward and phloem outward; cork cambium makes outer bark.
Identify trees by combining leaves, bark, slash, fruit and family features.
Khaya (Meliaceae) has pinnate leaves and capsules; Ficus (Moraceae) has milky latex and figs.
Binomial names give genus and species; family names end in -aceae.
Common names vary, so check accepted botanical names in a current database.

en.title: Forest Ecology: Organisms, Energy and Nutrients
en.short: Ecosystems, habitats, niches, food webs, energy flow, nutrient cycling, productivity and succession in forests.

sections.heading: Ecosystems, habitats, niches
sections.text: An ecosystem is a community of organisms plus the non-living environment, interacting as a system. A habitat is the place where a species lives, described by canopy cover, water, soil and other features. A niche is the species’ role and requirements: food, nesting place, activity time and interactions. Species can share a habitat but not an identical niche for long, because competition excludes one.

sections.heading: Energy and nutrients
sections.text: Energy enters a forest as sunlight. Producers, mainly trees and plants, convert it by photosynthesis into chemical energy. Gross primary productivity (GPP) is total energy captured; net primary productivity (NPP) is GPP minus plant respiration, the energy available to consumers. Energy moves along food chains, linear feeding sequences, and food webs, which link many chains. At each transfer energy is lost as heat, so top predators are few. Decomposers recycle nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus from litter and dead wood to the soil for roots.

sections.heading: Limiting factors and productivity
sections.text: A limiting factor is anything that restricts growth or survival, such as light, water, nutrients or predation. Liebig’s law of the minimum says growth is set by the scarcest resource. Shelford’s law of tolerance adds that too much or too little of a factor can limit a species. Productivity is the rate at which energy or biomass is produced; it varies with light, water, temperature and soil fertility.

sections.heading: Succession and management
sections.text: Ecological succession is the gradual change in species composition. Primary succession starts on bare substrate without soil, such as bare rock or lava; secondary succession follows disturbance such as logging or fire, where soil remains. Pioneer species arrive first, then seral (intermediate) stages, and a climax community is the supposed stable end point. Ecologists now treat climax as a range of states, not a single endpoint, because disturbance keeps changing forests. In a moist forest reserve in Nigeria, Chidi’s community protects a stream buffer and leaves dead wood; these habitats support frogs and birds while timber is harvested elsewhere. Management uses these ideas: maintain habitat diversity, connectivity and limiting resources, and monitor succession after harvest.

keyPoints: An ecosystem includes living organisms and their non-living environment interacting as a system.
A habitat is where a species lives; a niche is its role and requirements.
Energy flows one way through food chains and webs and is lost as heat at each transfer.
Decomposers recycle nutrients, so forest soils depend on litter and dead wood.
NPP = GPP minus plant respiration; limiting factors and productivity shape forest growth.
Succession runs from pioneer to seral to climax, but climax is not always a single fixed state.

en.title: Soils and Site Quality for Forests
en.short: Soil formation, profile, texture, water, nutrients, acidity, degradation and site quality for forests.

sections.heading: Formation and profile
sections.text: Soil forms from parent material through weathering. Climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time control the process, and human use can change it. A soil profile is a vertical section through the soil. Horizons are layers in the profile: O is organic litter, A is topsoil rich in humus, E is a leached layer, B is subsoil where material accumulates, C is weathered parent material and R is bedrock. Not every soil has every horizon.

sections.heading: Texture, structure and water
sections.text: Texture is the proportion of sand, silt and clay. Structure is how particles stick into aggregates. Porosity is the fraction of soil volume that is pore space. Water drains by gravity, is held in capillaries, or is bound too tightly for roots. Field capacity is water left after drainage; wilting point is where plants can no longer extract water. Available water lies between them. Example: field capacity 0.30 and wilting point 0.12 over 0.5 m of roots give available water = (0.30 − 0.12) × 0.5 = 0.09 m, or 90 mm.

sections.heading: Life, nutrients and acidity
sections.text: Organisms decompose organic matter, mix soil and form aggregates. Mycorrhizal fungi help roots obtain phosphorus and water. Organic matter stores nutrients and raises cation exchange capacity (CEC), the ability to hold positively charged nutrients. Nutrient availability depends on pH, CEC, leaching and texture. Acid soils may have aluminium toxicity and low phosphorus; liming raises pH. Degradation includes erosion, compaction, nutrient depletion, salinity and acidification. It lowers site quality.

sections.heading: Site quality and wildlife
sections.text: Site quality is the potential of a site to grow trees. It is often measured by site index, the dominant tree height at a reference age for a species. Climate supplies heat, light and rainfall; soil supplies water, air and nutrients; topography modifies both. For wildlife, soil and climate determine plant growth, cover, fruit and prey. This sets carrying capacity, the maximum population an area can support without lasting damage. Management can improve or damage these links.

keyPoints: Soil forms from parent material under climate, organisms, relief and time; human use also matters.
A profile has O, A, E, B, C and R horizons, though not every soil has all of them.
Texture is sand, silt and clay proportions; structure is aggregation; porosity is pore fraction.
Available water = (field capacity − wilting point) × root depth; porosity = 1 − bulk density ÷ particle density.
Organic matter and CEC hold nutrients; pH controls availability, and acid soils may need liming.
Site quality combines climate, soil and topography; it sets tree growth and wildlife carrying capacity.

en.title: Forest Meteorology and Microclimate
en.short: Solar radiation, forest microclimate, growth, fire, wildlife and carbon storage.

sections.heading: Climate drivers
sections.text: Solar radiation is the energy that drives the forest. Leaves absorb light for photosynthesis; its amount changes with latitude, season and cloud cover. Temperature controls growth, respiration and evaporation. Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air; high humidity slows evaporation from leaves and soil. Wind moves heat, water vapour and seeds, and increases water loss. Rainfall supplies soil water. These drivers vary by day, season and place, so the same forest can experience different conditions.

sections.heading: Forest microclimate
sections.text: A microclimate is the local climate near the ground, inside a stand or under a canopy. A forest modifies its microclimate. The canopy intercepts sunlight and rain, so less light and water reach the floor. Shade lowers daytime temperature, while canopy and litter reduce heat loss at night. Roots and litter help soil absorb rain, and transpiration adds water vapour, raising humidity. Trees slow wind, making the air calmer. These effects are strongest in dense, multi-layered forest and weaker in open woodland.

sections.heading: Growth, fire, wildlife
sections.text: Tree growth depends on light, warmth, water and nutrients working together. Too little rain or too much heat can close stomata, the leaf pores, and slow photosynthesis. Fire risk rises when fuel is dry, humidity is low, temperature is high and wind is strong. Wildlife behaviour follows microclimate: animals use shade to avoid heat, bask in sun, seek damp refuges, or move when rain and wind change. A canopy gap can create a warmer, drier patch that suits some plants and insects but not others.

sections.heading: Climate change and carbon
sections.text: Climate change is altering temperature, rainfall and fire weather. Some species may grow faster where water and nutrients allow; others face drought, heat, pests and fire. Forests store carbon in wood, roots, litter and soil. A growing forest removes carbon dioxide from the air; a burnt or degraded forest can release it. The carbon fraction of dry biomass is often about half, but it varies. Management, species and disturbance decide whether a forest is a carbon sink or source.

keyPoints: Solar radiation, temperature, humidity, wind and rainfall together control forest conditions.
A forest canopy intercepts light and rain, lowers daytime temperature, raises humidity and slows wind.
Tree growth needs light, warmth, water and nutrients together.
Dry fuel, low humidity, high temperature and strong wind raise fire risk.
Wildlife uses shade, sun, damp refuges and calm air, so microclimate affects behaviour.
Forests store carbon in biomass and soil, and can be a sink or a source depending on management and disturbance.

en.title: Forest Biometrics and Mensuration Mathematics
en.short: Forest arithmetic, geometry, statistics, probability and simple tests for tree and wildlife data.

sections.heading: Forest calculations
sections.text: Mensuration uses geometry. Basal area at breast height is A = πd² ÷ 4, where d is diameter. For a cylindrical stem, volume V = A × h = πr²h, with r radius and h height. Algebra rearranges formulas, for example h = V ÷ A. Logarithms solve exponential growth, y = ae^kt, so ln y = ln a + kt. Arithmetic keeps units consistent: use metres before reporting cubic metres.

sections.heading: Data and intervals
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise field data. For tree growth, diameters 20, 24, 28 and 32 cm, mean = (20+24+28+32) ÷ 4 = 26 cm. Squared deviations from 26 are 36, 4, 4 and 36; their sum is 80. Sample variance s² = 80 ÷ (4−1) = 26.67 cm², so s = √26.67 = 5.16 cm. Report n, mean, s and range for wildlife counts and yields. Probability p is the long-run proportion of times an event occurs. A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic over repeated samples; for a mean, its standard deviation is the standard error SE = s ÷ √n. For large n, an approximate 95% confidence interval for a mean is x̄ ± 1.96 SE. With n = 100, mean yield 30 m³/ha and s = 5, SE = 5 ÷ √100 = 0.5, so the interval is 30 ± 0.98, or 29.02 to 30.98 m³/ha.

sections.heading: Simple tests
sections.text: A t-test compares a mean with a value or two means. The one-sample statistic is t = (x̄ − μ) ÷ SE, with degrees of freedom n − 1. A chi-square test compares observed counts O with expected counts E: χ² = Σ[(O − E)² ÷ E]. Use it for categories such as seedling survival by treatment. State the null hypothesis, choose a significance level, usually 0.05, and compare the statistic with the critical value or p-value. Reject the null only when evidence is strong, and report the result plainly.

keyPoints: Basal area is A = πd² ÷ 4 and cylindrical stem volume is V = A × h = πr²h.
Mean is x̄ = Σx ÷ n; sample variance is s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) and standard deviation is s = √s².
Standard error is SE = s ÷ √n, and an approximate 95% confidence interval for a large sample mean is x̄ ± 1.96 SE.
A one-sample t-test uses t = (x̄ − μ) ÷ SE with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
A chi-square test uses χ² = Σ[(O − E)² ÷ E] to compare observed and expected counts.
Logarithms linearise exponential growth because y = ae^kt becomes ln y = ln a + kt.

en.title: Forest Surveying, Mapping and Remote Sensing
en.short: Compass, chain, tape, clinometer and level; map scale and contours; aerial photos; GIS and satellite images.

sections.heading: Ground measurements
sections.text:
Surveying fixes positions on the ground and puts them on a map. A chain or tape measures distance; keep it horizontal, or correct for slope. A compass gives bearing, the angle clockwise from north. Magnetic north differs from map north by magnetic declination, so check the map value. A clinometer measures vertical angle, and a level with a staff measures height difference.

Worked example: a tape gives slope distance 50 m to a tree and the clinometer reads 10°. Height difference = 50 × sin 10° = 50 × 0.1736 = 8.7 m. A plot 20 m by 30 m has area 600 m² = 0.06 ha, since 1 ha = 10,000 m². For irregular plots, split them into triangles or use offsets from a baseline.

sections.heading: Maps, scale and contours
sections.text: A map is a scaled drawing. Scale is the ratio of map distance to ground distance. At 1:10,000, 1 cm on the map represents 10,000 cm, or 100 m, on the ground. Contours join points of equal elevation. Closely spaced contours mean steep ground; widely spaced ones mean gentle ground. Contour interval is the height change between neighbouring contours.

sections.heading: Aerial photos, GIS and satellites
sections.text: An aerial photograph is taken from above; a stereopair, two overlapping photos, shows height and slope. Interpretation means identifying features by tone, texture, shape and pattern. A geographic information system (GIS) stores map layers with coordinates and analyses them, for example overlaying forest cover on roads. Satellite images add repeated coverage; resolution is the ground size of one pixel. Always ground-truth: check the map against the field.

keyPoints: Bearing is measured clockwise from north; correct for magnetic declination.
Height difference = slope distance × sin(vertical angle).
Area in hectares = area in m² ÷ 10,000.
Scale 1:10,000 means 1 cm on the map is 100 m on the ground.
Close contours mean steep slopes; the contour interval is the height step.
GIS overlays map layers; satellite pixels have a fixed ground resolution.

en.title: Tree Physiology and Vegetative Propagation
en.short: How trees gain and use resources, control growth, and are raised from seed or clones.

sections.heading: Energy and water
sections.text: Photosynthesis uses light, carbon dioxide and water to make sugars and release oxygen. It occurs in leaves, in chloroplasts containing chlorophyll. Respiration breaks down sugars with oxygen to release usable energy, carbon dioxide and water. Transpiration is water vapour loss through stomata, the leaf pores. It cools the leaf and helps pull water up the xylem, the water-carrying tissue. Roots absorb water and minerals through root hairs and mycorrhizal fungi, fungi that partner roots.

sections.heading: Hormones and dormancy
sections.text: Plant hormones are chemical signals. Auxins promote cell elongation, root formation and apical dominance, where the leading shoot suppresses side shoots. Cytokinins promote cell division and shoot growth. Gibberellins promote stem elongation and can break seed dormancy. Abscisic acid promotes dormancy and closes stomata in drought. Ethylene affects ripening, ageing and stress. Flowering responds to internal signals and the environment, especially day length and temperature. Dormancy is a resting state that helps trees survive cold or drought.

sections.heading: Seed handling
sections.text: A seed contains an embryo, stored food and a seed coat. Collect mature seed from healthy trees, avoiding insect damage. Test samples for purity, moisture and viability. Germination and tetrazolium tests check viability; the tetrazolium test stains living tissue. Orthodox seed tolerates drying and cool storage. Recalcitrant seed must stay moist and cool and lives only a short time. Pretreatment breaks dormancy: scarification scratches or softens a hard coat; stratification is cold, moist storage; soaking or gibberellin may help. Methods vary by species.

sections.heading: Vegetative methods
sections.text: Vegetative propagation makes a new plant from a parent without seed, so the offspring are clones, genetically identical to the parent. A cutting is a piece of stem, root or leaf placed in a moist medium; auxin may help rooting. Marcotting, or air layering, wounds a stem, wraps it in moist material and waits for roots before detaching it. Grafting joins a scion, the desired shoot, to a rootstock, the rooted base; their cambium layers must meet. Clonal forestry uses these methods; growers raise cuttings from superior trees but keep several clones to maintain genetic diversity.

keyPoints: Photosynthesis stores light energy in sugars; respiration releases it.
Transpiration pulls water up the xylem and cools leaves.
Auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, abscisic acid and ethylene control growth, flowering and dormancy.
Orthodox seed is stored dry and cool; recalcitrant seed must stay moist and cool.
Pretreatment such as scarification or stratification breaks seed dormancy.
Cuttings, marcotting and grafting produce clones, so clonal forestry must keep enough genetic diversity.

en.title: Forest Nursery Practice and Silvicultural Systems
en.short: Covers nursery layout, media, sowing, watering, shading, hardening, hygiene, outplanting and silvicultural systems.

sections.heading: Nursery layout and media
sections.text:
A forest nursery is where seedlings are raised for outplanting. Choose a site near reliable water, with level, well-drained ground and good access. Lay out beds and paths so workers can move and water easily. Keep compost, tools and waste away from beds.

Potting media (the material roots grow in) should be light, well drained and fertile. A common mix is topsoil, sand and composted organic matter, but local materials and trials decide the ratio. Keep media and beds clean to reduce damping-off, a fungal disease that kills young seedlings.

sections.heading: Sowing to hardening
sections.text:
Sow seed at the depth and spacing recommended for the species. Small seed is pressed into the surface and covered lightly; larger seed is covered more deeply. Mulch conserves moisture until germination. Water gently with a fine spray in the morning, keeping the medium moist but not waterlogged. Shade young seedlings from strong sun, then reduce shade gradually.

Hardening prepares seedlings for field conditions. Reduce watering and shade step by step over the last weeks, but do not let seedlings wilt badly. Nursery hygiene means clean tools and hands, weed control, removal of diseased plants and avoiding overcrowding.

sections.heading: Outplanting and aftercare
sections.text:
Outplant at the start of the rainy season. Dig a hole wider than the root ball, place the stem base at ground level, firm the soil and mulch.

Aftercare includes weeding, replacing failures and protecting seedlings from fire, livestock and pests.

sections.heading: Silvicultural systems
sections.text:
Silvicultural systems are plans for harvesting and regenerating a stand, a group of trees. Clear-felling removes all trees in one area and gives even-aged regeneration (trees of similar age). Shelterwood removes trees in stages, leaving shelter for seedlings. Selection removes mature trees singly or in small groups, giving uneven-aged forest (mixed ages).

Natural regeneration relies on seed fall or coppice (sprouts from cut stumps). Taungya lets farmers grow crops among young trees; they weed and tend the trees, and rules vary by country. Enrichment planting puts desirable seedlings into understocked forest.

keyPoints: A nursery needs reliable water, good drainage, clean beds, shade and a layout that separates production, compost and storage.
Potting media should be light, well drained and fertile, and hygiene reduces damping-off and pest spread.
Water gently, shade young seedlings, then harden them by gradually reducing water and shade before outplanting.
Outplant at the start of the rainy season, keep the stem base at ground level, firm the soil, mulch and weed.
Clear-felling removes all trees, shelterwood removes trees in stages, and selection removes mature trees singly or in small groups.
Natural regeneration, taungya and enrichment planting are regeneration methods, and taungya rules vary by country.

en.title: Plantation Forestry and Industrial Plantations
en.short: Site-species matching, spacing, mixtures, exotics, costs, rotations, yield and thinning.

sections.heading: Matching species to site
sections.text: Site-species matching means choosing species whose climate and soil needs fit the site: rainfall, dry season, altitude, soil depth, drainage, pH and pest history. Use local trials and experience, not nursery performance alone. Exotics such as eucalypts and pines are often planted because they grow fast and give uniform wood, but they can fail on poor sites, spread, or suffer pests. Indigenous species may grow more slowly but are adapted, support biodiversity and supply local products. For fuelwood, choose fast coppicing species; for poles, straight stems; for industrial roundwood, volume and fibre.

sections.heading: Spacing and mixtures
sections.text: Spacing sets stocking, the number of trees per hectare. At 2.5 m × 2.5 m each tree has 6.25 m², so stocking is 10,000 ÷ 6.25 = 1,600 trees/ha. Closer spacing gives early volume and straight stems but more competition and cost; wider spacing suits large crowns. Mixed planting can spread risk and improve soil, but species must not compete too strongly.

sections.heading: Costs and rotation
sections.text: Establishment costs include site preparation, seedlings, planting, weeding, fire protection and roads. Plan rotation length by products: short for fuelwood, medium for poles, long for sawlogs. Compare costs with expected yield and price, using discounting, valuing future income today. Growth and yield prediction uses site index, height at a reference age, yield tables, expected volume by age, inventory and models, checked against local plots.

sections.heading: Thinning and short rotations
sections.text: Thinning removes trees to reduce competition and favour crop trees. Thin from below, removing suppressed and damaged trees first, and schedule by stocking or basal area, the cross-sectional area of stems at breast height. Short-rotation plantations use close spacing and coppice, regrowth from cut stumps, for fuelwood or biomass; harvest early, then manage stools.

keyPoints: Site-species matching compares species needs with rainfall, soil, drainage, pH and pest risk, using local trials.
Exotics often grow faster and more uniformly, but indigenous species may be better adapted and lower risk; choose by product and site.
Stocking (trees/ha) for square spacing = 10,000 ÷ (spacing in m × spacing in m); 2.5 m × 2.5 m gives 1,600 trees/ha.
Rotation length follows the product: short for fuelwood, medium for poles, long for industrial sawlogs.
Thinning removes suppressed trees to favour crop trees and can be scheduled by stocking or basal area.
Short-rotation plantations use close spacing and coppice, with early harvests and stool management.

en.title: Forest Protection: Pests, Diseases and Fire
en.short: Insect pests, fungal diseases, fire behaviour, prescribed burning, browsing and windthrow in tropical forests.

sections.heading: Insect pests and IPM
sections.text:
Insect pests damage leaves, shoots, bark or roots. The teak defoliator (Hyblaea puera) is a well known tropical example: its larvae strip teak leaves and outbreaks slow growth. Termites attack roots and stems. Most insects pass through egg, larva, pupa and adult; the larvae usually do the damage.

Control begins with monitoring and correct identification. Cultural methods include healthy planting stock, sanitation, wider spacing and mixed stands. Biological control uses predators, parasitoids and pathogens; Bacillus thuringiensis kills leaf-eating larvae. Integrated pest management (IPM) combines monitoring, damage thresholds, cultural and biological methods, and chemicals only when justified.

sections.heading: Fungal diseases
sections.text:
Fungal diseases enter through wounds, roots, leaves or seed. Damping-off, caused by soil-borne pathogens such as Pythium and Rhizoctonia, kills nursery seedlings in wet, crowded beds. Root and butt rots, for example Ganoderma and Armillaria, decay wood. Look for wilting, cankers, stained wood and fruiting bodies.

Spores spread in wind, rain, soil and on tools. Control uses clean seed and soil, drainage, wider spacing, removal of infected material, resistant species and rotation. Trichoderma is used as a biological control against soil-borne pathogens. IPM combines surveillance, cultural and biological measures with approved fungicides where needed.

sections.heading: Fire and physical damage
sections.text:
Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat. Causes include lightning, land clearing, hunting and escaped burns. Behaviour depends on fuel, weather and slope. Surface fires burn litter and undergrowth, crown fires reach the canopy, and ground fires smoulder in peat.

Prevention uses firebreaks, fuel reduction, early detection and public education. Prescribed burning is deliberate low-intensity fire under a written plan, used to reduce fuel and encourage regeneration; it needs permits, trained crews and the right weather.

Browsing by livestock and wild herbivores strips seedlings; fencing, guards and controlled hunting protect regeneration. Windthrow and storms topple trees, especially on shallow soils or after thinning; avoid exposed edges, keep shelter and salvage damaged timber quickly.

keyPoints: Identify the pest or pathogen and its life stage before choosing a control.
Larvae of defoliators such as Hyblaea puera cause the heaviest leaf loss.
IPM combines monitoring, thresholds, cultural, biological and chemical methods.
Damping-off is a nursery disease of wet, crowded beds; drainage and clean soil prevent it.
Fire behaviour depends on fuel, weather and slope; prescribed burning needs a plan, permit and trained crew.
Fencing and guards reduce browsing damage; exposed edges increase windthrow risk.

en.title: Tree Improvement and Seed Technology
en.short: Provenance trials, seed stands and orchards, selection, breeding values, genetic gain and seed supply.

sections.heading: Provenance and seed sources
sections.text: A provenance is the geographic origin of a seed lot. A provenance trial grows seed from several origins in one place, in replicated plots, to see whether differences are genetic and stable. A seed stand is a selected stand managed for seed collection; it is cheap but untested. A seed orchard is a planted collection of selected clones or families, isolated and managed for regular seed crops. Isolation reduces pollen contamination from outside trees. Orchards may be seedling or clonal, and untested or tested.

sections.heading: Selection and breeding
sections.text: Selection means choosing superior trees or families. A tree’s breeding value is its value as a parent, estimated from the performance of its progeny in trials, not from its own appearance alone. Controlled pollination makes known crosses: female flowers are bagged before opening, pollen is applied by hand, and bags stay until seed sets. Genetic gain is the expected improvement in the next generation. A simple breeder’s equation is R = h² × S, where S is the selection differential, how far the selected parents sit above the stand average, and h² is narrow-sense heritability, the share of variation that offspring inherit. If S = 4 m and h² = 0.25, R = 1 m. Clonal forestry plants tested clones; it captures more gain but needs several clones to limit risk.

sections.heading: Seed handling and supply
sections.text: Seed handling covers collection, extraction, cleaning, drying, storage, testing and certification. Orthodox seeds are dried and stored cold; recalcitrant seeds lose viability if dried and need short-term handling. Tests include germination, viability and moisture content. National seed services and forest tree seed centres supply tested seed, keep records, certify lots and advise on provenance choice. Seed lots should be labelled by species, provenance and test result. Rules differ by country, so check the current national service.

keyPoints: A provenance is the geographic origin of a seed lot; provenance trials compare origins in a common environment.
A seed stand is an untested selected stand; a seed orchard is a managed, isolated collection of selected clones or families.
Breeding value is estimated from progeny performance, not from the parent’s own appearance.
Controlled pollination uses bagging and hand pollination to make known crosses.
Genetic gain can be estimated as R = h² × S; with S = 4 m and h² = 0.25, R = 1 m.
Clonal forestry captures gain from tested clones but needs enough clones to limit genetic risk; seed services test and certify lots, and rules vary by country.

en.title: Forest Growth and Yield Modelling
en.short: Stand structure, site index, basal area, volume increment, sample plots, yield tables, density and growth models.

sections.heading: Stand structure and measures
sections.text: Stand structure is how trees are arranged: species mix, age, size classes, canopy layers and spacing. Even-aged stands have one main age class; uneven-aged stands have several. Basal area is the cross-sectional area of stems at breast height (1.3 m), summed per hectare (m²/ha). Volume is estimated from dbh (diameter at breast height), height and a volume equation or table. Increment is change over time. Periodic annual increment (PAI) is change divided by years; mean annual increment (MAI) is total volume divided by age.

sections.heading: Site index and plots
sections.text: Site index is the mean height of dominant and codominant trees at a reference age. It measures site quality for one species, and the reference age varies by country and species, so state it. Permanent sample plots (PSPs) are marked, mapped plots where trees are tagged and measured, then remeasured every few years. They record dbh, height, mortality and new trees, so growth can be estimated without confusing it with site differences. Temporary plots show only the current state.

sections.heading: Yield tables and density
sections.text: Yield tables give expected volume, basal area and tree numbers by age and site index, usually for dense, fully stocked stands. They are guides, not exact forecasts for a particular stand. Stand density management uses spacing and thinning to control competition. Density can be described by trees per hectare, basal area or a density index. Thinning removes some trees, often the poorer or surplus stems, and concentrates growth on the best ones.

sections.heading: Models and cutting cycles
sections.text: Growth and yield models forecast timber supply. Whole-stand models predict stand averages; individual-tree models predict each tree; process-based models use physiology. They help set the allowable cut (the sustainable harvest) and the cutting cycle, the interval between harvests in a stand. Example: 400 trees/ha with mean dbh 30 cm. Basal area = 400 × (π/4 × 0.30²) = 28.3 m²/ha. If volume rises from 280 to 325 m³/ha in 5 years, PAI = 45 ÷ 5 = 9 m³/ha/yr.

keyPoints: Basal area per hectare = trees per hectare × (π/4 × DBH²), with DBH in metres.
PAI = (V2 − V1) ÷ (t2 − t1); MAI = V ÷ age.
Site index is top height at a stated reference age for a named species, mainly in even-aged stands.
Permanent sample plots are tagged and remeasured to measure true growth.
Yield tables describe fully stocked stands and must be adjusted for actual density.
Growth models forecast supply and help set allowable cuts and cutting cycles.

en.title: Forest Inventory and Sampling Design
en.short: Sampling theory, sample size, plot and point methods, stratification, NTFPs, wildlife and error estimation.

sections.heading: Sampling and sample size
sections.text:
Forest inventory estimates a population from a sample. The sampling frame lists the units. Simple random sampling gives every unit equal chance; systematic sampling takes fixed intervals; stratified sampling divides the population into homogeneous strata. Sampling error comes from the sample; non-sampling error from measurement, recording or access.

For a mean, n = t² s² ÷ E², where t is the t-value, s the pilot standard deviation and E the allowable absolute error. For relative error e, n = t² CV² ÷ e², with CV = s ÷ mean. Example: CV = 30%, e = 10%, t = 2. n = (4 × 900) ÷ 100 = 36 plots. Check: 4 × 900 = 3600; 3600 ÷ 100 = 36. Use pilot CV and allow for non-response.

sections.heading: Plot, strip, point and line
sections.text: A fixed-area plot is a measured area, often circular or square, where trees above a diameter limit are recorded. A strip is a long narrow plot, useful in dense or linear vegetation. Point sampling, or angle-count sampling, uses a prism or angle gauge at a point; a tree is counted if its apparent width exceeds the gauge. This is variable-radius sampling: each counted tree represents a fixed basal area per hectare (the basal area factor), and the counting radius increases with tree diameter, so trees are sampled with probability proportional to their basal area. Line sampling counts intersections along a line, useful for downed wood, canopy cover or ground cover.

sections.heading: Stratification, error and assessments
sections.text:
Stratification by land cover, age, site or ownership makes strata uniform and lowers variance; allocate more samples to large or variable strata. Non-timber forest products (NTFPs) such as fruit, bark, resin and medicinal plants are patchy, so quadrats or transects within strata are common. Wildlife is mobile and detection is imperfect, so define the sampling unit and observation method and estimate detection probability.

Report estimates with standard error, the estimate’s standard deviation, and confidence intervals. National forest assessments use stratified samples, remote sensing and permanent plots; local management inventories use finer strata and smaller errors. Methods vary by country; check official definitions.

keyPoints: Sampling error falls as sample size rises; non-sampling error does not.
For a mean, n = t² s² ÷ E²; for relative error, n = t² CV² ÷ e².
Fixed-area plots sample equal areas, while variable-radius point sampling samples trees with probability proportional to basal area.
Stratification lowers variance when strata are more uniform than the whole population.
NTFP and wildlife inventories must record the sampling unit, effort and detection probability.
Report estimates with standard error and confidence intervals, and check current national methods.

en.title: Forest Economics and Valuation of Forest Goods
en.short: Timber and NTFP economics, stumpage, forest rent, Faustmann rotation, ecosystem service valuation and forestry CBA.

sections.heading: Timber, stumpage and rent
sections.text: Timber is valued from delivered log prices. Stumpage is standing-tree value, usually the price paid to the owner for the right to harvest. It equals delivered price minus harvesting, transport and marketing costs, so remote stands can have low stumpage. Non-timber forest products (NTFPs) such as fruit, honey and medicine are often gathered with little capital and sold locally or used at home, so their value is easily missed. Forest rent is annual net income from forest land after costs.

sections.heading: Rotation and soil expectation
sections.text:
The rotation is the age at which a stand is harvested. Soil expectation value (SEV), or land expectation value, is the value of bare land under perpetual rotations. Ignoring annual costs, SEV = [R − C(1+i)^T] ÷ [(1+i)^T − 1], where R is harvest revenue at age T, C is planting cost at year 0 and i is the discount rate. The Faustmann rotation maximises SEV; it is usually shorter than the rotation that maximises mean annual increment. NPV, internal rate of return and benefit-cost ratio are related tests.

Example: i = 5%. Rotation A: T = 30, R = 10,000, SEV = 10,000 ÷ (1.05^30 − 1) = 3,010. Rotation B: T = 25, R = 8,000, SEV = 8,000 ÷ (1.05^25 − 1) = 3,352. B is preferred.

sections.heading: Valuing ecosystem services
sections.text: Ecosystem services are benefits people get from forests. Watershed protection is often valued by avoided cost or replacement cost, such as treating water if forest cover is lost. Carbon is valued using a carbon price or social cost of carbon per tonne of CO2 equivalent; these vary by country and year, so check the official source. Recreation is valued by travel cost or contingent valuation. Avoid double counting.

sections.heading: Cost-benefit analysis
sections.text: Cost-benefit analysis compares discounted benefits and costs. NPV = Σ (B_t − C_t) ÷ (1+r)^t. Accept a project if NPV > 0, or if benefit-cost ratio > 1. Use sensitivity analysis because prices and non-market values are uncertain.

keyPoints: Stumpage is the standing-tree value, usually delivered log price minus harvesting, transport and marketing costs.
Forest rent is annual net income from forest land after costs.
SEV = [R − C(1+i)^T] ÷ [(1+i)^T − 1] for harvest revenue R, planting cost C at year 0, rotation T and discount rate i, ignoring annual costs.
The Faustmann rotation is the rotation with the highest SEV.
NPV = Σ (B_t − C_t) ÷ (1+r)^t; accept a project if NPV > 0.
Watershed, carbon and recreation values use avoided cost, replacement cost, carbon price, travel cost or contingent valuation, and carbon prices vary by country and year.

en.title: Forest Policy, Legislation and Administration
en.short: How forest policy is made, forest law and reserves, tenure and access, and Nigeria’s forestry bodies.

sections.heading: Policy and its cycle
sections.text: Forest policy is a government’s statement of goals, principles and priorities for forests, trees and wildlife, often with targets and instruments. It is not a single law. It is made through a policy cycle: a problem is recognised and put on the agenda; options are formulated with stakeholders; a decision is adopted; the policy is implemented through laws, budgets and institutions; and it is monitored and reviewed. Policy may be national, state or local, and can be influenced by international agreements, markets and community demands.

sections.heading: Law, reserves, tenure
sections.text: Forest law is the body of statutes, regulations and subsidiary rules that gives legal force to policy. It creates forest reserves, defines offences, sets penalties and powers, and controls felling, hunting and access. A forest reserve is land legally set aside for forestry; it may be wholly state-owned or include community rights. Land tenure is the set of rules by which land is owned, held or used. In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in state governors, while customary tenure still shapes access. Access rights are rights to enter and use a forest, such as collecting fuelwood or grazing, and may be customary, permitted or denied.

sections.heading: Nigeria and a case
sections.text:
In Nigeria, forestry is mainly a state matter. State forestry departments or ministries manage state forest reserves, issue permits and enforce state forestry laws. The Forestry Research Institute of Nigeria (FRIN), based in Ibadan, conducts forestry research. The National Park Service manages national parks. Laws and institutions differ by country and change, so check the current state forestry law and gazette.

Case: a state proposes to convert part of a reserve to farmland. The forestry department applies the reserve law, communities claim customary access, and the state reviews its policy. The outcome depends on the law, consultation and political decision.

keyPoints: Forest policy sets goals and priorities for forests and wildlife, while forest law gives policy legal force.
Policy is made through a cycle of agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation and review.
Forest law creates reserves and controls felling, hunting and access.
Land tenure and access rights decide who may own, enter and use forest land, and may be customary or statutory.
In Nigeria, state forestry departments manage state reserves, FRIN conducts forestry research and the National Park Service manages national parks.
Forest laws and regulations differ by country and change over time, so check the current official text.

en.title: Wildlife Ecology and Population Dynamics
en.short: Habitat, home range, migration, population parameters, abundance methods, carrying capacity and sustainable offtake.

sections.heading: Habitat, range and behaviour
sections.text:
Habitat is the resources and conditions a species needs: food, water, cover, space and special sites such as nests or mineral licks. Habitat quality affects survival and breeding. A home range is the area used in normal activities; a territory is the defended part. Ranges may overlap and shift with season and food.

Migration is regular seasonal movement between areas, often to track food or breeding conditions. Behaviour includes social grouping, activity rhythm, breeding and dispersal, a one-way movement from the natal area. These affect where animals are and how easy they are to count.

sections.heading: Population parameters
sections.text:
Population size N changes through four parameters: N(t+1) = N(t) + births − deaths + immigrants − emigrants. Natality is birth rate, mortality death rate, immigration movement in and emigration movement out. Births and deaths are internal; immigration and emigration link populations.

Rates are per head per year, for example 0.2 births per female per year. Density-dependent factors such as food act more strongly as N rises; density-independent factors such as drought act regardless of N.

sections.heading: Estimating abundance
sections.text:
Direct counts count animals directly. They suit large, visible species but depend on detection. Capture-recapture marks M animals, then samples n and records R marked. If marks are not lost and animals are equally catchable, Lincoln-Petersen gives N = M × n ÷ R. Example: mark 40, catch 50, 10 marked; N = 40 × 50 ÷ 10 = 200.

Distance sampling counts animals along lines or points and records distance. Detection declines with distance; a detection function estimates density. Dung or spoor (tracks and signs) counts record signs on plots or transects. They are indirect indices needing calibration: density = dung density × decay rate ÷ defecation rate.

sections.heading: Carrying capacity and offtake
sections.text:
Carrying capacity K is the population an area can sustain long term. Logistic growth is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K). Maximum sustainable yield is rK/4 at N = K/2.

Sustainable offtake is harvest kept within production and adjusted by monitoring.

keyPoints: Habitat provides food, water, cover and space; home range is the area used, while territory is defended.
Population change = births − deaths + immigration − emigration.
Lincoln-Petersen estimate: N = M × n ÷ R, assuming a closed, well-mixed population with equal catchability.
Distance sampling estimates density from detection declining with distance; dung and spoor counts are indirect indices needing calibration.
Carrying capacity K is the long-term sustainable population; logistic growth is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K).
Maximum sustainable yield in the logistic model is rK/4 at N = K/2; real offtake is set conservatively and monitored.

en.title: Wildlife Management and Habitat Manipulation
en.short: Sustained yield, culling, cropping, translocation, habitat burning, water and community wildlife areas.

sections.heading: Sustained yield principles
sections.text:
Sustained yield, or sustainable yield, means taking animals at a rate the population can replace. Managers estimate population size, growth rate and carrying capacity, the maximum number an area can support.

Culling removes animals to reduce numbers or damage. Cropping is a planned harvest, often for meat or trophies. Translocation moves animals to a new area, for restocking or to relieve pressure. Problem animal control reduces damage to crops, livestock or people, using fencing, scaring, capture or, as a last resort, killing the animal. Set quotas from census data and review them each season.

sections.heading: Habitat manipulation
sections.text:
Prescribed burning removes old grass and encourages fresh growth, but the season, frequency and intensity must suit local species. Water provision can support animals in dry periods, yet fixed water points may concentrate grazing and spread disease, so placement and rotation matter.

Reseeding sows native or useful forage plants after disturbance. Encroachment control keeps farmland, settlements and invasive plants out of wildlife areas. Monitor results and adjust.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
The logistic model gives maximum sustainable yield (MSY) as MSY = rK ÷ 4, where r is the intrinsic growth rate, the per-head growth rate under ideal conditions, and K is carrying capacity.

If K = 1,000 animals and r = 0.2 per year, MSY = (0.2 × 1,000) ÷ 4 = 50 animals per year. Real quotas are usually set below MSY and revised after census.

sections.heading: Ranches and community areas
sections.text:
Ranches and game farms manage wild animals for meat, trophies or breeding, often combining wildlife with livestock.

Community wildlife areas give local people rights and benefits from wildlife, which can improve tolerance and enforcement. In all cases, clear management plans, regular monitoring and fair benefit sharing are essential.

keyPoints: Sustained yield means harvesting no more than the population can replace.
Culling reduces numbers, cropping is a planned harvest, translocation moves animals, and problem animal control reduces damage.
Set quotas from census data and review them each season.
Prescribed burning, water provision, reseeding and encroachment control are main habitat tools, but each needs monitoring.
Logistic maximum sustainable yield is MSY = rK ÷ 4; with K = 1,000 and r = 0.2, MSY = 50 animals per year.
Ranches, game farms and community wildlife areas need clear plans, monitoring and fair benefit sharing.

en.title: Protected Areas and Conservation Planning
en.short: This summary covers categories, design, zoning, corridors, buffers and transfrontier conservation in Africa.

sections.heading: Categories
sections.text: Countries give protected areas legal names, but the IUCN system is a common guide. A national park (IUCN category II) protects ecosystems for conservation, education and recreation, with extractive use normally banned. A game reserve protects wildlife and may allow controlled hunting or tourism. A forest reserve is land set aside for timber, watershed or soil protection; it is not automatically a biodiversity reserve. A sanctuary is a smaller site managed for particular species or habitats, often strictly. In Nigeria, Cross River and Gashaka-Gumti are national parks, Omo is a forest reserve, and Afi Mountain is a wildlife sanctuary. Yankari in Bauchi began as a game reserve, was upgraded to a national park, and was later handed back to Bauchi State as a game reserve.

sections.heading: Design and zoning
sections.text: Design should represent the main ecosystems and species, be large and compact where possible, include natural boundaries, and replicate populations so one disaster does not wipe out a species. Zoning separates strict protection from use. A core zone limits entry to research and patrol; a buffer zone allows controlled use such as gathering or tourism; a transition zone supports community land uses. Buffer zones reduce edge effects, where sunlight, wind and human access alter forest interior.

sections.heading: In-situ and ex-situ
sections.text: In-situ conservation keeps species in their natural habitat: protected areas, community reserves and corridors. Ex-situ conservation keeps them outside it: seed banks, botanical gardens, zoos and captive breeding. Ex-situ is a backup, not a substitute, because it holds few individuals and loses ecological context. For trees, seed banks and living collections conserve genetic resources.

sections.heading: Connectivity and borders
sections.text: Wildlife corridors are strips of habitat that let animals move between patches, maintaining gene flow and access to seasonal resources. Transfrontier conservation areas link protected areas across borders. The Great Limpopo Transfrontier Park joins Kruger in South Africa, Limpopo in Mozambique and Gonarezhou in Zimbabwe. The Kavango-Zambezi area links five countries. Such plans need shared rules, patrols and community benefits, or they remain lines on a map.

keyPoints: National parks, game reserves, forest reserves and sanctuaries have different legal aims; a forest reserve is not automatically a biodiversity reserve.
Good design represents ecosystems, is large and compact, and replicates populations.
Zoning usually separates a strict core, a controlled buffer and a community transition zone.
In-situ conservation protects species in their habitat; ex-situ conservation is a backup outside it.
Corridors maintain movement and gene flow between habitat patches.
Transfrontier conservation needs shared management and community benefits, not only cross-border boundaries.

en.title: Wildlife Census, Monitoring and Law Enforcement
en.short: Field methods for counting wildlife, analysing the data, and enforcing wildlife law.

sections.heading: Counting animals in the field
sections.text: A census counts a population once; monitoring repeats counts to detect change. Line transects suit many mammals and birds: the observer walks a line, records each animal and its perpendicular distance, and distance sampling corrects for animals missed far from the line. Aerial surveys cover large areas quickly for big mammals but undercount animals under canopy. Camera traps record shy, nocturnal species; captures per 100 trap-nights (a trap-night is one trap set for one night) give an index, and individually recognisable animals allow capture-recapture estimates. Call counts and point counts suit birds and frogs; reptiles are found by visual encounter surveys, cover boards or pitfall traps. Field guides and signs (tracks, dung, calls) aid identification.

sections.heading: Recording and analysing counts
sections.text:
Record date, time, GPS position, observer, species, group size, distance and angle, and always record effort: kilometres walked, hours or trap-nights. A count without effort cannot be compared with another.

Worked example. Two transects of 2 km each, strip half-width 25 m, 12 animals seen.
Area sampled = 2 × L × w = 2 × 4,000 × 25 = 200,000 m² = 20 ha.
Density = 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6 animals per ha = 60 per km².
For a 150 km² zone: 60 × 150 = 9,000 animals.

sections.heading: Patrols and intelligence
sections.text: Enforcement relies on ranger patrols planned by intelligence, not routine. Patrol-based monitoring records where patrols went and what they found (snares, camps, gunshots, carcasses), so finds can be compared with effort; SMART (Spatial Monitoring and Reporting Tool) is widely used software for this. Intelligence comes from informants, community contacts, seizure records and market surveys, and analysts map hotspots to target patrols. Community rangers and benefit-sharing reduce local support for poaching.

sections.heading: Evidence and illegal trade
sections.text:
Evidence must survive court. Photograph the scene, record GPS and time, label each item uniquely, and keep a written chain of custody naming everyone who handled it. DNA and isotope analysis can link meat or ivory to a species and region.

CITES, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, regulates international trade in listed species through permits; it entered into force in 1975. National laws differ, so check the current text. Bushmeat control combines market and road checks, snare sweeps and prosecution.

keyPoints: A census counts once; monitoring repeats counts to detect change, so effort must always be recorded.
Strip transect density: D = n ÷ (2Lw), where L is total line length and w the strip half-width.
Camera trap index = independent captures ÷ trap-nights × 100.
Individually recognisable animals allow capture-recapture; unmarked populations need distance sampling or indices.
Patrol data are useful only when patrol effort is recorded, so finds can be compared with effort.
Evidence needs a documented chain of custody, and CITES permits govern international trade in listed species.

en.title: Fisheries and Aquaculture in Forest Landscapes
en.short: Fish biology, breeding, stock assessment, pond construction, fingerlings, water quality and reserve fisheries.

sections.heading: Fish biology and breeding
sections.text: Major African freshwater fish include Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), African catfish (Clarias gariepinus) and Nile perch (Lates niloticus). Tilapia are mostly omnivorous cichlids; many carry eggs in the mouth (mouthbrooding). Catfish are hardy omnivores and predators, and can breathe air, so they survive low oxygen. Nile perch are predatory. In hatcheries, broodstock (adult fish kept for breeding) spawn naturally or receive hormones, especially catfish. Fry eat microscopic plants and animals (phytoplankton and zooplankton); supplementary feed must be protein-rich for growth.

sections.heading: Stock assessment
sections.text: Stock assessment estimates how many fish can be caught without depleting the stock. Catch per unit effort (CPUE) is catch ÷ fishing effort; falling CPUE may mean overfishing, but gear and effort must be recorded. Mark-recapture uses the Lincoln-Petersen formula N = (M × C) ÷ R, where M fish are marked, C are caught later and R are marked. Example: M = 200, C = 250, R = 40, so N = (200 × 250) ÷ 40 = 1,250. This assumes a closed population, marked fish mix, and no mark loss.

sections.heading: Ponds, water and fingerlings
sections.text: Pond siting needs clay soil that holds water, a reliable water supply, gentle slope and an inlet and outlet. Build dykes (embankments) and keep depth suitable; shallow ponds warm quickly but risk overheating. Fingerlings are young fish for stocking. Produce them from broodstock, spawning, nursery and grading (sorting by size). Water quality must be tested: dissolved oxygen, temperature, pH, ammonia and turbidity. Low oxygen or high ammonia kills fish. Feed according to total fish weight and remove uneaten feed.

sections.heading: Fisheries in reserves
sections.text: In forest reserves and protected wetlands, fisheries need management plans. Common tools are permits, closed seasons (fishing bans), mesh-size limits, no-take zones (areas closed to fishing) and community co-management. Rules differ by country, so check the current national wildlife or fisheries law. Monitor catch, effort and water quality, and protect spawning grounds and bankside vegetation.

keyPoints: Tilapia, African catfish and Nile perch are major African freshwater fish with different feeding and breeding habits.
Broodstock produce fingerlings through spawning, nursery and grading; catfish often need hormone-induced breeding.
CPUE = catch ÷ effort, and falling CPUE can signal overfishing if effort and gear are recorded.
Lincoln-Petersen estimate: N = (M × C) ÷ R, assuming a closed, well-mixed population with no mark loss.
Pond site, clay soil, water supply, dykes and inlet/outlet determine success; test dissolved oxygen, pH, temperature and ammonia.
Fisheries in forest reserves and protected wetlands need permits, closed seasons, mesh limits, no-take zones and community co-management, under national law.

en.title: Apiculture and Beekeeping
en.short: Honey bee biology, hive products, apiary siting, colony and swarm management, harvesting and pollination.

sections.heading: The bee colony
sections.text: Apiculture is beekeeping. A colony is a family with one queen, many workers and some drones. The queen lays eggs. Workers are female and do foraging, building, nursing and guarding. Drones are male and mate with new queens. Workers and queens come from fertilised eggs, and larval diet decides caste. Drones come from unfertilised eggs. Workers communicate food location by dances. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. Honey bees pollinate, but so do stingless bees, solitary bees, hoverflies, butterflies, moths, birds and bats.

sections.heading: Hives and siting
sections.text: Hives are shelters beekeepers provide. Traditional hives include log, clay and basket hives with fixed combs. Movable-frame hives, such as the Langstroth, let the beekeeper lift frames out. Top-bar hives are simpler movable-comb hives. Site an apiary, where hives stand, with forage, water, shade and a windbreak. Keep it accessible, away from homes and livestock, and above flood level. Avoid fields sprayed with insecticide while bees forage.

sections.heading: Management and swarms
sections.text: Colony management means inspection, giving space before crowding, controlling pests and diseases, feeding when nectar is scarce and replacing a failing queen. Swarming is colony reproduction: the old queen leaves with part of the workers. Crowding and a strong nectar flow encourage it. Prevent swarming by adding supers (extra boxes), splitting the colony into a new nucleus, or removing queen cells early. Removing cells alone only delays swarming. A nucleus is a small colony with a queen, workers and young.

sections.heading: Harvest and pollination
sections.text: Harvest honey only from capped combs (cells sealed with wax), and leave enough stores. Work at dusk or dawn, use little smoke, uncap cells, extract in a spinner, strain and settle before bottling. Do not overheat honey; keep moisture low or it ferments. Hive products include honey, beeswax, propolis (plant resin collected by bees), pollen, royal jelly (queen food). Amina in Oyo State, Nigeria, keeps Langstroth hives near a cashew plot. She adds supers before the flow, splits a crowded colony, and harvests only capped combs. Her bees pollinate cashew and forest trees.

keyPoints: A honey bee colony has one queen, female workers and male drones; caste is set by larval diet.
Pollination is pollen transfer from anther to stigma, and many insects, birds and bats are pollinators.
Langstroth and top-bar hives allow comb inspection; traditional hives use fixed combs.
Site apiaries with forage, water, shade and windbreak, away from people, livestock and pesticide spray.
Swarming is colony reproduction; prevent it by giving space, splitting colonies or early queen-cell removal.
Harvest only capped honey, leave stores, and keep honey dry and not overheated.

en.title: Non-Timber Forest Products and Agroforestry
en.short: NTFPs such as gum, rubber, rattan, bushmeat and honey, plus agroforestry systems and their livelihood and soil benefits.

sections.heading: What NTFPs are
sections.text: Non-timber forest products (NTFPs) are forest goods other than industrial timber. Examples are gum arabic from Acacia senegal, natural rubber from Hevea brasiliensis, rattan stems, bushmeat, medicinal plants, honey and mushrooms. Rural households use or sell them. Harvesting should leave enough plants and animals to regenerate. Wildlife and forest laws, which vary by country, regulate hunting and some collection.

sections.heading: Harvesting and processing
sections.text: Gum arabic is tapped by shallow bark cuts; the gum hardens, is picked, cleaned, dried and graded. Rubber is tapped by a thin spiral cut; latex is collected, coagulated, rolled into sheets and dried or smoked. Rattan stems are cut, stripped, cleaned and dried; heat helps bending. Honey is drained from combs, strained and stored sealed, without strong heating. Mushrooms are cleaned and dried only after safe identification, because poisonous kinds exist. Medicinal plants are dried and stored dry; bark and roots are taken sparingly. Bushmeat is often smoked or dried, but hunting must follow quotas and bans and carries disease risks.

sections.heading: Agroforestry systems
sections.text: Agroforestry is the deliberate growing of trees or shrubs with crops or animals on the same land. In alley cropping, hedgerows of trees such as Leucaena or Gliricidia are planted between crop strips. Prunings are spread as mulch or green manure, adding organic matter and nitrogen and reducing erosion; roots and shade can compete with crops. Home gardens are layered mixtures of trees, vegetables, herbs and medicines near the house. Parkland trees are scattered trees in farmland, as with Faidherbia albida and shea in West African Sahel parklands.

sections.heading: Livelihoods and soil
sections.text: Trees on farms support livelihoods through fruit, nuts, gum, fodder, fuelwood, honey and medicine, and spread income across seasons. Many improve soil: legumes fix nitrogen, deep roots take up nutrients from lower layers, and litter and shade protect the surface. In a Sahel parkland, Amina keeps Faidherbia albida and shea trees among millet; she collects shea nuts and uses prunings as mulch. Benefits depend on species, spacing, rainfall and market access.

keyPoints: NTFPs are forest goods other than industrial timber, such as gum arabic, rubber, rattan, bushmeat, medicinal plants, honey and mushrooms.
Harvesting must leave enough parent plants and animals to regenerate, and hunting and collection are regulated by national laws.
Simple processing includes tapping and drying gum, coagulating and smoking rubber, cleaning and drying rattan, straining honey, and drying mushrooms after safe identification.
Agroforestry deliberately combines trees or shrubs with crops or animals on the same land.
Alley cropping uses tree hedgerows and prunings as mulch or green manure; home gardens and parkland trees are other common systems.

Trees on farms support livelihoods and soil fertility through products, nitrogen fixation by legumes, litter, mulch, shade and erosion control, but competition and local conditions affect the benefits.

en.title: Forest Hydrology and Watershed Management
en.short: How forests affect water movement, erosion and catchment planning.

sections.heading: Water pathways
sections.text: Interception is rain caught by leaves, branches and litter; much of it evaporates before reaching the soil. Infiltration is water entering the soil surface. Runoff is water that flows over the surface or in channels. Streamflow is the water carried by streams; it comes from quick storm flow and slower baseflow released from groundwater. Groundwater recharge is water that percolates deep enough to refill an aquifer.

sections.heading: Forest and cleared land
sections.text: Forest cover usually raises interception and, if the soil is undisturbed, infiltration. It reduces surface runoff and erosion, and it can help sustain baseflow by storing and releasing water slowly. But trees also transpire, so a forest may yield less total water than short vegetation. On cleared land, compaction and bare soil lower infiltration, so more rain becomes overland flow. This can cause flash floods, soil loss, less groundwater recharge and lower dry-season flow. The effects depend on climate, soil, slope, species and how the land is managed.

sections.heading: Survey and erosion control
sections.text: A watershed survey maps the catchment boundary, slopes, soils, land use, streams and erosion sites using topographic maps, GPS and field checks. Erosion control keeps soil covered, spreads runoff, and treats gullies from the head down. Common works are contour drains, check dams, grass strips and revegetation. For example, a footpath on a slope can concentrate runoff and start a gully. The plan is to divert the water into a protected drain, plant the gully head and keep grass cover.

sections.heading: Buffers and plans
sections.text: Riparian buffer strips are vegetated zones beside streams. They filter sediment and nutrients, stabilise banks and shade water. A catchment management plan sets agreed land uses and works to protect water quality, manage water yield and reduce flood risk. It needs stakeholders, monitoring and review. Forests and buffers slow runoff, but they cannot prevent extreme floods; plans must combine land use, drainage and storage.

keyPoints: Forests usually increase infiltration and reduce erosion, but may reduce total water yield through transpiration.
Cleared land often increases overland flow and erosion and lowers dry-season baseflow.
A watershed survey maps boundary, slope, soils, land use, streams and erosion sites.
Gully control works from the head down and spreads runoff.
Riparian buffers filter pollutants and stabilise banks.
Catchment plans need stakeholder agreement and monitoring.

en.title: Forest Roads, Engineering and Harvesting Operations
en.short: Planning, drainage and stream crossings of forest roads, plus harvesting, machines and safety.

sections.heading: Road planning and alignment
sections.text: Forest roads are engineered tracks that carry timber, workers and equipment. Planning starts with the harvest area, traffic, soil and slope. Alignment is the route in plan and profile. Keep roads on stable ground, avoid wet soils and steep side slopes, and use gentle grades. Grade = rise ÷ run × 100. Example: a rise of 12 m over 150 m is 12 ÷ 150 × 100 = 8%. Steep grades increase erosion and vehicle risk. Use cut-and-fill carefully and revegetate bare ground.

sections.heading: Drainage and streams
sections.text: Water must leave the road quickly without scouring it. Side drains, cross drains and culverts carry runoff to stable outlets. Stream crossings are the most sensitive points. Minimise their number, cross at right angles, keep banks stable, and size culverts for peak flows. Fords and bridges need local engineering advice. Sediment from roads harms fish and water supplies. Roads also fragment habitat, create edge effects and give hunters access, so plan closures and buffers.

sections.heading: Harvesting operations
sections.text: Harvesting includes felling, extraction, loading and transport. Felling is cutting the standing tree; extraction is moving logs to a landing, a hard standing where logs are sorted and loaded. Plan felling direction, escape routes and exclusion zones. Use skid trails or cable systems suited to slope and soil. Load within vehicle limits and secure loads. Wet weather and steep ground raise soil damage, so use timing and mats where appropriate.

sections.heading: Machines and safety
sections.text: Chainsaws need training, personal protective equipment (PPE), a pre-use check and a sharp chain. Kickback is the sudden upward throw of the saw; hold it firmly and use the chain brake. Never work alone; have someone within sight or shout distance. Tractors and winches need stable ground, guards and safe zones. A winch stores energy in the cable, so keep people clear and never straddle a cable. Follow local law and employer rules; these vary by country.

keyPoints: Forest roads must be planned for traffic, soil, slope and water.
Grade = rise ÷ run × 100; keep grades gentle and drain runoff to stable outlets.
Stream crossings need minimal number, stable banks and culverts sized for peak flow.
Roads cause erosion, sedimentation, habitat fragmentation and access for hunting.
Harvesting sequence: felling, extraction to a landing, loading, transport.
Chainsaw and winch work require training, PPE, exclusion zones and local safety law.

en.title: Wood Science and Forest Products Utilisation
en.short: Wood structure, moisture, strength, seasoning, products, grading, storage and decay control.

sections.heading: Structure and properties
sections.text: Wood is a cellular material. Its walls contain cellulose microfibrils in a matrix of hemicellulose and lignin. Softwoods are mostly tracheids; hardwoods also have vessels and fibres.
