Density is mass per unit volume, often oven-dry mass divided by green volume. Strength generally rises with density and falls as moisture rises below fibre saturation. Durability varies with species and extractives; heartwood is usually more durable than sapwood. Shrinkage is anisotropic: tangential shrinkage exceeds radial, and longitudinal is least.

sections.heading: Moisture and shrinkage
sections.text: Moisture content (MC) = (wet mass − oven-dry mass) ÷ oven-dry mass × 100. Above the fibre saturation point, about 25 to 30% for many species but variable, water is free in cell cavities. Below it, bound water leaves and wood shrinks. Example: wet mass 1,200 g, oven-dry 800 g gives (1,200 − 800) ÷ 800 × 100 = 50% MC. A green board 200 mm wide that dries to 190 mm has shrunk (200 − 190) ÷ 200 × 100 = 5%. Actual shrinkage depends on species and direction.

sections.heading: Seasoning and products
sections.text: Air seasoning is slow and cheap but depends on weather; kiln seasoning uses controlled temperature, humidity and air flow to dry faster without severe defects. Sawmilling breaks logs into boards, with kerf loss and tension to manage. Plywood glues thin veneers with grain crossed; particleboard presses resin-bonded chips. Pulp and paper separate fibres mechanically or chemically. Charcoal is made by pyrolysis, and fuelwood is a major product.

sections.heading: Grading, storage, decay
sections.text: Grading sorts timber by strength, defects and moisture for a stated use. Store timber level, stickered (stacked with small spacer sticks for air flow), covered and ventilated. Decay fungi need wood, oxygen, moderate temperature and moisture above about 20%; wet soil contact is risky. Control by drying, ventilation, raising timber off ground, avoiding soil contact and using preservatives. Check local grading rules and preservative standards.

keyPoints: Moisture content = (wet mass − oven-dry mass) ÷ oven-dry mass × 100.
Shrinkage is greatest tangentially, less radially and least along the grain.
Strength rises with density and with drying below fibre saturation.
Air seasoning is cheap and slow; kiln seasoning is faster and controlled.
Plywood crosses veneer grain; particleboard bonds chips with resin.
Decay needs moisture, oxygen and suitable temperature; keep timber dry and off soil.

en.title: Forest Entomology: Insects and Forest Health
en.short: Insect orders, life cycles, damage, monitoring, thresholds and integrated control in forests.

sections.heading: Orders and life cycles
sections.text: Forest insects are grouped by order. Coleoptera (beetles), Lepidoptera (moths), Hymenoptera (sawflies, ants, parasitoids) and Diptera (flies) have complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult. The larva does most feeding. Hemiptera (true bugs), Orthoptera (grasshoppers) and Isoptera (termites) have incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph, adult. Termites also have castes: workers, soldiers and reproductives. Identification matters because each order and stage needs different survey and control methods.

sections.heading: Damage types
sections.text: Borers tunnel into bark, phloem or wood. They cut transport channels, weaken stems, cause stain and let fungi enter. Defoliators, mainly moth and sawfly larvae, eat leaves and buds; heavy or repeated loss reduces photosynthesis, growth and sometimes survival. Termites feed on dead wood, roots and living trees, and are serious in plantations and dry wood. Sap-sucking pests such as aphids and scale insects pierce tissues, remove sap, cause yellowing, distortion, honeydew and sooty mould, and may transmit pathogens.

sections.heading: Survey and thresholds
sections.text: Monitoring means regular, recorded sampling. Use fixed plots or transects, counts on sample trees, frass and exit holes, damage scores, and traps such as pheromone, light or sticky traps. Record weather and natural enemies. The economic injury level is the pest density at which the cost of control equals the loss it prevents; the economic threshold, or action threshold, is the density at which control is applied, usually set below the injury level. Example: if control costs 20,000 money units and each pest unit causes 100 money units loss, the injury level is 20,000 ÷ 100 = 200 pest units. Check local prices and methods.

sections.heading: Integrated control
sections.text: Integrated pest management combines methods, using pesticides only when monitoring shows need. Silviculture includes suitable species, mixed stands, spacing, thinning, pruning and removing infested material. Resistant planting uses provenances or clones with lower susceptibility. Natural enemies include parasitoids, predators and pathogens; conserve them by reducing broad-spectrum sprays and keeping habitat. Careful pesticide use means the correct product, dose, timing and target, with rotation to slow resistance, and protection of pollinators and beneficials. Pesticide rules vary by country, so check the national regulator and label.

keyPoints: Coleoptera, Lepidoptera, Hymenoptera and Diptera have complete metamorphosis; Hemiptera, Orthoptera and Isoptera have incomplete metamorphosis.
Borers tunnel wood, defoliators remove leaves, termites feed on wood, and sap-suckers pierce tissues and may transmit pathogens.
Monitoring uses fixed samples, damage signs and traps, with records of weather and natural enemies.
Economic injury level = control cost ÷ loss caused per pest unit; apply control at the economic threshold (action threshold), set below the injury level.
Integrated control combines silviculture, resistant planting, natural enemies and careful pesticide use.
Pesticide registration and rules vary by country, so check the national regulator and label.

en.title: Forest Pathology: Causes, Diagnosis and Management
en.short: Causes, spread, resistance, diagnosis and management of tropical tree diseases.

sections.heading: Causes and the disease triangle
sections.text: Tree disease is harm caused by a pathogen or abiotic factor. Fungi commonly cause rots, wilts, cankers and leaf spots, and spread mainly by spores. Bacteria cause wilts, blights and galls and spread in water, rain splash and wounds. Viruses cause mosaic, mottle and distortion and spread by sap, insects or infected planting material. Nematodes are tiny roundworms; some feed on roots and cause decline, and some carry viruses. Drought, waterlogging, poor nutrition and herbicide injury can mimic disease. The disease triangle says disease needs a susceptible host, a pathogen able to infect it, and a favourable environment.

sections.heading: Spread, resistance and diagnosis
sections.text: Infection spreads by wind, rain, soil water, root contact, insects, tools, seed and nursery stock. Trees resist by bark and waxy cuticles, wound closure, killing infected cells in a hypersensitive response, and induced chemicals. In wood, compartmentalisation limits decay: the tree walls off injured or infected tissue rather than healing it. Diagnosis starts with field history and symptoms. Symptoms are the plant’s response, such as yellowing or rot; signs are the pathogen itself, such as mycelium, spores or ooze. Tropical examples: damping-off by Pythium or Rhizoctonia, root rot by Ganoderma or Phellinus, wilt by Fusarium or Ceratocystis, leaf spots by Colletotrichum or Pestalotiopsis. Check roots, cut bark, incubate samples, use microscopy and molecular tests where available. Koch’s postulates are used to confirm that a suspected pathogen causes a disease.

sections.heading: Nursery and stand management
sections.text: Nursery control is prevention: clean seed, sterile media, raised beds, drainage, correct sowing depth, spacing, ventilation, and morning watering. Remove and destroy diseased seedlings; do not reuse contaminated trays or soil. Fungicides may help damping-off but cannot cure established root rot. In plantations, match species and provenance to the site, use resistant stock where available, avoid wounds, prune correctly, thin for airflow, drain wet sites, and remove infected debris and stumps. In natural stands, favour mixed species and natural regeneration, monitor trails and edges, and restrict movement of infected wood and soil. Clean tools and quarantine reduce new introductions.

keyPoints: The disease triangle links a susceptible host, an infective pathogen and a favourable environment.
Fungi are the main causes of tree rots, wilts, cankers and leaf spots; bacteria, viruses and nematodes also cause disease.
Symptoms are the plant’s response; signs are the pathogen itself.
Trees resist through bark, wound closure, hypersensitive responses, induced chemicals and compartmentalisation in wood.
Nursery disease control is mainly preventive: clean seed and media, drainage, spacing, ventilation and removal of diseased seedlings.
Plantation and natural-stand management uses resistant stock, site matching, wound avoidance, thinning, sanitation, mixed species and quarantine.

en.title: Professional Ethics, Extension and Community Forestry
en.short: Duties, professional codes, extension methods, participation, benefit sharing and conflict in community forestry.

sections.heading: Duties and codes
sections.text: A forestry and wildlife professional serves the public, the landowner and the resource. To the public: honesty, safety, transparency and stewardship of environmental values. To the landowner or community: act within authority, obtain free, prior and informed consent, keep confidences, disclose conflicts of interest and give fair advice. To the resource: sustainable use, maintaining regeneration, soil, water and biodiversity, and monitoring effects. Professional bodies publish codes of ethics. They commonly require competence, continuing education, truthful reporting, respect for law and local rights, and no misrepresentation. Codes differ by country and body; read the current code for your practice.

sections.heading: Extension and participation
sections.text: Extension is informal education bringing research to forest users. Methods include visits, group meetings, demonstrations, field days, farmer field schools, radio and mobile messages. Match method to message, literacy, language, distance and cost. A demonstration is better shown than described; radio reaches many quickly but cannot answer every question. Good extension listens, uses local examples and records feedback. Community participation means involving local people in planning, decisions, work and monitoring, not merely informing them. It is stronger when people share real authority and when customary and statutory tenure are understood.

sections.heading: Sharing, conflict, design
sections.text: Benefit sharing sets clear rules for who receives timber, non-timber products, fees, carbon payments or tourism income, and how costs are shared. Put agreements in writing, in local languages, with accounts open to members. Conflict resolution maps parties and interests, then uses dialogue, mediation, agreed rules and an appeal route. Design a project by assessing needs and tenure, identifying stakeholders, setting measurable objectives, agreeing institutions and rules, budgeting and monitoring. Include women, youth and forest-dependent groups. Case: a village beside a reserve wants fuelwood and grazing. Extension staff hold a field day, map both uses, and help users zone a woodlot and a grazing path. The committee writes sharing and mediation rules; monitoring checks regeneration and reports back.

keyPoints: A professional owes honesty and stewardship to the public, informed consent and fair dealing to the landowner, and sustainable use to the resource.
Professional codes commonly require competence, truthful reporting, respect for law and local rights, and disclosure of conflicts of interest.
Extension is two-way informal education; match the method to the message, literacy, language and cost.
Community participation must give local people real influence in planning, decisions and monitoring.
Benefit-sharing agreements should be written and transparent, with accounts open to members.
Conflict resolution maps interests and uses dialogue, mediation and agreed rules; project design starts with needs, tenure and stakeholders.

en.title: Research Methods and the Undergraduate Project
en.short: Framing research, design, data, statistics and reporting for the final project or field trip.

sections.heading: Framing the problem
sections.text: Start with a research problem: a gap in knowledge that matters and can be studied within your time and resources. A literature review is a critical summary of what is known; read widely, compare findings and identify the gap. Keep a record of every source. State objectives as specific, measurable actions, for example to compare seedling survival under two shade levels. A hypothesis is a testable prediction, often written as a null hypothesis (no difference) and an alternative. Objectives say what you will do; hypotheses say what you expect.

sections.heading: Design and data
sections.text: Experimental design plans treatments, controls, replication (repeated units), randomisation (chance allocation) and blocking (grouping similar units) so that effects can be separated from chance. Choose field or laboratory methods from standard protocols, calibrate instruments, obtain permits and follow safety and ethics rules. Record data at once in a notebook or datasheet, with units, dates, site and observer. Use a clear coding system and back up files. Decide the analysis before collecting data.

sections.heading: Analysis and writing
sections.text: Basic statistics describe data: mean (average), median (middle value), range (highest minus lowest) and standard deviation (spread). And test hypotheses: t-test (compare two means), chi-square (compare counts), correlation (association). Check assumptions and report sample size, test and p-value (probability under the null). Scientific writing uses clear sections: introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Cite every borrowed idea in one consistent style such as author-date and list full references. Avoid plagiarism. Plan the project with a timeline, budget, risk assessment and regular supervisor meetings. A field trip report adds itinerary, observations and site description.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Seedling heights in centimetres: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. Mean = 70 ÷ 5 = 14 cm. Deviations are −4, −2, 0, 2, 4; squares sum to 40. Sample variance = 40 ÷ (5−1) = 10, so sample standard deviation = √10 ≈ 3.16 cm. Report units and n = 5. A hypothesis test would compare groups and give a p-value.

keyPoints: Define a research problem as a gap that matters and is feasible within your resources.
Objectives state what you will do; hypotheses state testable expectations, often as null and alternative.
Good design uses controls, replication, randomisation and blocking.
Record data immediately with units, dates, site and observer, and back up files.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample standard deviation = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)].
Write in a clear scientific structure, cite every borrowed idea consistently and plan the project with a timeline and supervisor meetings.

en.title: Forest Biotechnology and Molecular Tools
en.short: Tissue culture, molecular markers, GM limits and gene banks for forest genetic resources.

sections.heading: Clonal propagation
sections.text:
Tissue culture means growing small plant explants on sterile nutrient medium under controlled conditions. Micropropagation multiplies a selected tree through axillary buds, producing clones. Somatic embryogenesis makes embryo-like structures from somatic cells, which can become plantlets.

These methods mass-produce elite trees chosen for growth, form or disease resistance. A Ghanaian plantation programme might micropropagate one resistant clone, then field-test it before wide planting. Limits include contamination, cost, maturation problems, somaclonal variation and the need for field trials.

sections.heading: Markers and diversity
sections.text:
Molecular markers are DNA or protein variants that reveal genetic differences. Early work used isozymes; modern studies use microsatellites (SSR) or single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). A provenance is a geographic source population. In provenance studies, markers can check whether planting stock comes from the claimed source and how populations differ. Diversity assessment reports allelic richness, heterozygosity and differentiation.

Markers have limits. Neutral markers may not reflect adaptive variation, and small samples give biased estimates. Results depend on sampling design and laboratory quality.

sections.heading: Genetic modification
sections.text:
Genetic modification (GM) changes a tree’s genetic material, often using Agrobacterium-mediated transformation or gene editing. Traits studied include pest resistance, altered lignin and sterility to limit gene flow. The principles resemble crop GM: identify a trait, insert and regulate the gene, regenerate plants, then test biosafety.

Limits are serious. Trees are long-lived and outcrossing, so gene flow and ecological effects are hard to predict. Regulations differ by country, and public acceptance varies. GM trees need confined field trials, monitoring and approval before release.

sections.heading: Conservation banks
sections.text:
Seed banks store orthodox seeds dry and cold after testing viability. Recalcitrant seeds, which die on drying, need cryopreservation, tissue culture or field collections. Gene banks may also hold DNA, pollen and living trees. Good conservation samples many populations across a species range, not one stand.

A national forest institute might bank seeds from several provenances of a valuable species, record collection data and regenerate samples periodically. Follow national plant genetic resource rules and any adopted international standards.

keyPoints: Tissue culture grows explants on sterile medium; micropropagation and somatic embryogenesis produce clones for mass propagation.
Elite clones need field testing because somaclonal variation and maturation can reduce gains.
Molecular markers such as SSR and SNP can verify provenance and estimate allelic richness, heterozygosity and differentiation.
Neutral markers may not reveal adaptive variation, so sampling design matters.
GM trees face gene-flow, biosafety and country-specific regulatory limits.
Seed and gene banks conserve forest genetic resources; recalcitrant seeds need cryopreservation or tissue culture.

en.title: Forest Landscape Restoration and Degraded Land Recovery
en.short: Diagnosing degradation and deforestation, landscape restoration principles, ANR, planting design and monitoring.

sections.heading: Degradation and deforestation
sections.text:
Forest degradation is a loss of structure or function in land that still has tree cover. Deforestation is the conversion of forest to another land use. The drivers differ by region: in parts of West and Central Africa, smallholder clearance for farming, fuelwood cutting and logging are common; elsewhere large-scale agriculture, mining, fire and roads dominate.

Diagnosis means measuring the change, not guessing it. Field plots and satellite imagery show canopy cover, biomass and species mix. A nearby reference site shows what the land could support, so the gap between the two defines the restoration target.

sections.heading: Landscape principles
sections.text:
Forest landscape restoration (FLR) is a planned process that regains ecological integrity and improves human well-being across a mosaic of land uses, agreed with the people who use the land. It is not the same as planting trees everywhere.

The principles are: work at landscape scale; use the original cover as a reference, not a blueprint; restore the greater part of the landscape, not isolated patches; and weigh costs against benefits. Natural regeneration is usually cheaper and more diverse than planting, so it is tried first where seed sources and rootstock survive.

sections.heading: Techniques and damaged sites
sections.text:
Assisted natural regeneration (ANR) removes what blocks natural regrowth: weeding around seedlings, and protection from grazing and fire, sometimes with enrichment sowing. Reforestation plants trees on land that recently held forest; afforestation plants on land that did not.

Design covers species matched to the site, spacing, and purpose such as timber, soil cover or habitat. On mined sites, first stabilise the spoil, then test and amend the soil, then plant hardy pioneer species. On eroded sites, contour structures slow runoff before trees go in.

sections.heading: Monitoring and commitments
sections.text:
Monitor whether the site is recovering, using simple indicators: survival, canopy cover, height and species richness, later biomass and soil. Compare with a baseline and repeat at fixed intervals.

The Bonn Challenge, launched in 2011, invites countries to restore degraded and deforested land; AFR100 is a related African Union-led initiative that contributes African pledges to the Bonn Challenge. The UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration runs from 2021 to 2030. Pledge figures and rules change, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: Degradation is loss of function under tree cover; deforestation is conversion to another land use.
Diagnose with plots, imagery and a reference site before choosing a treatment.
FLR works across a whole landscape and balances ecology with livelihoods.
Prefer assisted natural regeneration where seed sources and rootstock survive.
Match species to site and stabilise soil before planting mined or eroded land.
Monitor survival, cover and diversity against a baseline at fixed intervals.

en.title: Climate Change, Carbon Accounting and REDD+
en.short: Forest carbon pools, measurement, baselines, MRV, additionality, leakage and REDD+ safeguards.

sections.heading: Gases and forest carbon
sections.text:
The main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O), compared as carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) using global warming potential. In the forest carbon cycle, photosynthesis moves CO2 into biomass; respiration, decomposition, fire and harvest return it. Pools are aboveground biomass, belowground biomass, dead wood, litter and soil organic matter.

Stocks come from field plots. Diameter and height feed allometric equations with wood density and carbon fraction, often 0.47 to 0.5 of dry mass. Dead wood uses line transects, litter quadrats, soil cores by depth with bulk density. Remote sensing maps area and change but needs field calibration.

Worked example: 100 tonnes dry biomass × 0.47 = 47 tonnes carbon. 47 × 44 ÷ 12 = 172.3 tonnes CO2e. The 44/12 ratio is the molecular mass ratio of CO2 to carbon.

sections.heading: Baselines and MRV
sections.text:
A baseline is the counterfactual emissions expected without the project or policy, set from historical data, models or regional benchmarks, documented and kept conservative. REDD+ means reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation, plus conservation, sustainable forest management and enhancement of carbon stocks. Under the UNFCCC, countries report forest reference emission levels and safeguards information.

Monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) measures results, reports them and has them checked independently. Projects follow standards such as Verra VCS or Gold Standard. Additionality means reductions would not have happened without the project; tests include legal requirement, barriers and investment. Leakage is emissions displaced outside the boundary and must be estimated and deducted. Permanence risk matters.

sections.heading: Safeguards and tenure
sections.text: REDD+ and carbon projects need social and tenure safeguards. These include recognition of customary and statutory land rights, free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) of Indigenous peoples and local communities, fair benefit sharing, biodiversity protection and accessible grievance mechanisms. The UNFCCC Cancun safeguards are widely used. National laws and project standards differ, so check the current national REDD+ safeguards. Weak tenure can cause conflict and failed projects; clear rights support lasting carbon outcomes.

keyPoints: Greenhouse gases are compared as CO2e using global warming potential.
Forest carbon pools are aboveground biomass, belowground biomass, dead wood, litter and soil organic matter.
Carbon stock = dry biomass × carbon fraction; CO2e = carbon × 44 ÷ 12.
A baseline is the counterfactual without the project; additionality and leakage must be tested and accounted for.
MRV measures, reports and independently verifies results against a standard.
REDD+ requires tenure and social safeguards, including FPIC and benefit sharing.

en.title: Conservation Genetics and Advanced Wildlife Science
en.short: Population genetics, viability modelling, disease ecology, conflict management and dissertation design.

sections.heading: Genetics in small populations
sections.text: Population genetics studies allele and genotype frequencies. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes an ideal large, randomly mating population; departures show that a force acts. Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency, strongest in small populations, and can fix or lose alleles. Inbreeding is mating between relatives; it raises homozygosity and can cause inbreeding depression by exposing harmful recessive alleles. Effective population size, Ne, is the size of an ideal population losing heterozygosity or accumulating inbreeding at the same rate. It is often far below the census count because of unequal sex ratio, variable family size and fluctuations. For Ne = 50, ΔF = 1/(2Ne) = 0.01 per generation. After 10 generations, F ≈ 1 − (1 − 0.01)^10 = 0.096, about 9.6%.

sections.heading: Markers and forensics
sections.text: Molecular markers are inherited DNA variants used to infer identity, relatedness and species. Microsatellites are highly variable short repeats; single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are single-base variants; mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited and useful for species and population assignment. DNA barcoding compares a standard gene region, commonly COI in animals, with reference libraries. In wildlife forensics, markers can identify species from meat, ivory, bone or hair, link a specimen to a population, detect hybrids and match individuals. Clean samples and validated reference data are essential.

sections.heading: Modelling and disease
sections.text: Population viability analysis (PVA) uses demographic models, often matrix or individual-based simulations, to estimate extinction risk under scenarios. Sensitivity analysis shows which vital rates matter most. Disease ecology studies host-pathogen dynamics: transmission, reservoirs, spillover and immunity. In wild animals, density, social contact, season and human interfaces shape outbreaks; surveillance and One Health approaches link wildlife, livestock and people.

sections.heading: Conflict and research
sections.text: Human-wildlife conflict management starts with the drivers: crop damage, predation, competition for land and unsafe waste. Measures include guarding, fencing, diversion, compensation and community-based planning, but each needs monitoring. A master’s dissertation should ask a focused question, state hypotheses, choose a sampling design with adequate power, obtain ethics and permit approval, and plan reproducible data analysis.

keyPoints: Effective population size Ne is usually smaller than census size.
Inbreeding rises by ΔF = 1/(2Ne) per generation in an ideal population.
Genetic drift is stronger in small populations and can fix or lose alleles.
Microsatellites, SNPs and mitochondrial DNA support species identification and wildlife forensics.
Population viability analysis estimates extinction risk and sensitivity to vital rates.
Disease ecology and conflict management require surveillance, community engagement and monitoring.
